Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2025-11-28 15:00 UTC
- Duration: ~52 minutes
- Recording: yes
- Attendees: Evan Morales (Redwood AE), Priya Khatri (Redwood SE), Tom Alvarez (GreenWave Infra), Sara Lin (GreenWave ML), Maya Kapoor (GreenWave SRE), Raj Patel (Product)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be fuzzy):
Redwood walked through workload-aware scheduler knobs for continuous batching, max_num_seqs, token caps and how KV cache hit rate affects RPS and p95 latency. Customer described on‑prem constraints (multi-tenant cluster, 4x A100-ish nodes behind VPC-like firewall). Action items: share knob playbook, run warm-cache stress test, schedule bench run.

Topics covered:
- Continuous batching behaviour under bursty RPS
- max_num_seqs and per-tenant token limits (prevention of head-of-line blocking)
- KV cache warmup strategies and prefix caching
- Quantization tradeoffs (int8 vs fp16) and kernel selection impact
- On‑prem network topology and cross-node KV fetch costs
- Fallback policies & graceful degradation when capacity is saturated

Transcript:
[00:00:05] Evan (Redwood AE): Hey everyone thanks for joining, we got about an hour, we thought we'd focus on the scheduler knobs that matter for your bursty telehealth workloads and also call out on-prem considerations — Priya will lead the technical parts.
[00:00:18] Tom (GreenWave): Yep thanks. Our main pain: p95 latency spikes when a batch of long transcripts arrive — 1 to 3 long calls interleaved with lots of short inference requests, and our current setup gets clogged.
[00:00:30] Priya (Redwood SE): Thanks Tom. Quick clarifying Q: are long calls mostly longer sequences (token lengths > 2k) or are you also seeing many short prompts in same queue?
[00:00:38] Sara (GreenWave): Mostly long seqs for transcription+summarization — the 2k+ is common, but we also have bursts of small assistant prompts from the mobile app.
[00:00:45] Priya: Okay. So two axes: sequence length distribution and RPS variance. For continuous batching, the scheduler's max_num_seqs and token cap are the knobs we tune to avoid head-of-line blocking.
[00:00:58] Raj (GreenWave): Can you define head-of-line blocking in this context?
[00:01:02] Priya: Sure — if a long sequence is batched early and the scheduler fills with sequences that have many remaining tokens, short requests behind it wait until that long sequence finishes generating. The fix is to limit per-sequence contribution to a batch (max_num_seqs) and then let short requests form their own batches.
[00:01:20] Evan: Another lever is adaptive windowing — shrink batch window when p50 latency rises above threshold, that helps for mixed workloads.
[00:01:28] Maya (SRE): Does that interact badly with throughput targets? We have contractual throughput and want to avoid large unit-cost increases.
[00:01:35] Priya: There's always a tradeoff. If you shrink windows aggressively you drop batching efficiency, increasing per-token cost. But we can set policies: keep latency SLO at 200ms p95 for web interactions and allow long jobs to use spare capacity or run on a dedicated queue.
[00:01:48] Tom: On-prem specifics — our cluster is behind a firewall, 4 nodes with A40/A100 class, NVSwitch inside each box, but cross-node is over 25Gb. KV cache is currently local per-node; cold misses cause cross-node fetch and we see a 2.5x latency hit.
[00:02:05] Priya: Yep that's expected. Two recommended patterns: 1) prefer node-local prefix caching for high-hit paths and schedule requests by routing affinity; 2) set a small remote-prefetch timeout so you don't block the request waiting for remote KV — serve a partial result or fall back to a lower-cost variant (smaller model quantized).
[00:02:22] Sara: So prefetch means we request remote KV async and if it arrives fast we stitch it in, otherwise continue?
[00:02:27] Priya: Exactly. Async prefetch with a threshold (e.g., 20ms) prevents tail latency blowups. It reduces p95 but might lower hitrate effective for long tails.
[00:02:35] [00:03:01] Unidentified Participant: There's background noise, sorry if I cut in.
[00:03:05] Priya: No worries. Back to max_num_seqs — the default we use in hosted configs is 64 for many medium-length workloads, but for very mixed it helps to set max_num_seqs to 8-16 and instead rely on higher concurrency to keep throughput.
[00:03:22] Evan: I'll add a sample mapping: short-only endpoints -> max_num_seqs 32, long-only batchers -> max_num_seqs 4 with longer token cap; mixed endpoints -> per-tenant queueing with adaptive windows.
[00:03:34] Tom: How about token caps? If someone sends 8k tokens in a single request do we chunk?
[00:03:38] Priya: We recommend hard token limits at the ingress (e.g., 4096) and server-side chunking for longer audio transcriptions — stream partial outputs. Chunking reduces scheduler pressure and keeps max seqs manageable.
[00:03:49] Sara: What about quantization? We tried int8 and saw 10-15% latency improvement but quality dips in rare cases.
[00:03:55] Priya: int8 helps inference speed and memory; fp16 still gives better stability for long-context models. One approach is mixed precision: fp16 for KV-indexing and int8 for final logits in non-critical paths. We'll send a short note on expected latency delta per model family.
[00:04:09] Raj: Is kernel selection automatic?
[00:04:12] Priya: The runtime chooses kernels based on seq length and hardware, but you can pin a kernel family if you want deterministic perf. Pinning helps debugging but often sacrifices best-case throughput.
[00:04:22] [00:05:00] Maya: We're multi-tenant and concerned about noisy neighbors. Any guidance for token caps per-tenant?
[00:05:06] Priya: Per-tenant token caps + soft priority queues are the typical solution. You can configure tenant-level token budgets per minute and a burst pool. Also useful: admission control that rejects or redirects very-long requests to background queues.
[00:05:20] Tom: How does Redwood handle fallbacks when dedicated capacity is hit?
[00:05:25] Evan: We have routing policies — prefer dedicated, then private pool, then hosted compatible lower-cost variants. For on‑prem you can set a policy to spill over to a smaller quantized model hosted in the cloud for non-sensitive data, or to a queued batch for async processing.
[00:05:39] Sara: We cannot send PHI to cloud. So any spillover must stay on-prem, which limits options.
[00:05:44] Priya: Understood — then best to reserve a small warm standby pool on-prem (even one machine) and use that for emergency spill. It's cheaper than full overprovisioning and helps latency.
[00:05:54] Raj: For capacity planning what metrics should we collect?
[00:05:58] Priya: Key ones: token distribution histogram (per minute), request size percentiles, KV cache hitrate by prefix and by node, queue length distribution, scheduler window wait times, and GPU utilization per-device. Also keep p50/p95/p99 latency for both generation and end-to-end app.
[00:06:12] Tom: We can provide token traces — Sara will export them.
[00:06:15] Sara: Yep will do.
[00:06:22] [00:12:48] Priya: Quick walkthrough of a sample config (we discussed knob names live; paraphrasing):
- scheduler.max_num_seqs: limit of sequences per batch (lower prevents hogging)
- scheduler.max_token_contribution: max tokens a single request can contribute to a batch
- scheduler.max_batch_delay_ms: cap on how long to wait for a batch to fill
- scheduler.adaptive_window: percentiles-based shrink/expand logic tied to p50/p95
- kv.prefetch_timeout_ms: when to give up on remote KV and continue
- admission.token_rate_limit: tenant-level token budget and burst pool

Priya: For your on‑prem cluster, try initial tune: max_num_seqs=12, max_token_contribution=512, max_batch_delay_ms=12, kv.prefetch_timeout_ms=20. That gives a good balance for mixed telehealth workloads.
[00:12:58] Tom: Any rough numbers on expected p95 improvement?
[00:13:02] Priya: In our bench, these settings reduced p95 from ~740ms to ~210–300ms for mixed workloads with a warm cache; p50 stayed stable and throughput dropped 8–12% from ideal perfect batching.
[00:13:12] Evan: Important caveat: those numbers assume high KV hitrate (~80%+). With cold cache the p95 can spike to multiples because of remote fetch.
[00:13:22] Sara: How do we improve KV hitrate?
[00:13:26] Priya: Several levers: prefix caching at ingress (store commonly observed prefixes), increase cache size for hot prefixes, and proactively pre-warm cache for scheduled batches (e.g., when you expect a bunch of long calls). Also consider LRU tuning and segmenting cache by tenant.
[00:13:39] Tom: Does segmenting mean we reserve a portion of KV for each tenant?
[00:13:42] Priya: You can partition logically so hot tenants don't evict each other's prefixes. There's a memory tradeoff but it helps tail latency.
[00:13:49] Raj: On the pre-warm idea — can we trigger pre-warm at the start of clinic hours?
[00:13:53] Priya: Yes, schedule pre-warm jobs to touch expected prefixes; that warms local caches. We can provide a script that converts your day-of-week traces into a warmup set.
[00:14:00] [00:20:05] Evan: Let's talk about instrumentation — we recommend per-request tags: model, seq_len, tenant_id, route, batch_id, kv_hit boolean. These make it trivial to slice tail latency causes.
[00:20:16] Maya: Are these tags heavy on storage? We have limited observability budget.
[00:20:20] Evan: You can sample at 1% for full traces and 100% for aggregated counters. The per-token counters are small, full traces only on error or periodic sample.
[00:20:29] Priya: Also enable token-level cost breakdowns in the console; that helps correlate cost spikes with config changes.
[00:20:36] [00:27:40] Sara: About quantization again — if we use int8 everywhere, what are the KV memory savings?
[00:27:45] Priya: Rough ballpark: int8 reduces model memory ~2-3x depending on quant scheme and gains proportional for KV entries. But int8 can increase soft errors for long-context attention; recommended to validate on your eval set. We'll share test harness suggestions.
[00:27:58] Tom: For on‑prem networking, is RDMA needed for cross-node KV? We don't have it.
[00:28:03] Priya: RDMA helps, but not required. If you don't have RDMA, ensure lower-latency NICs and keep remote fetches async. Avoid designs that block on remote fetch synchronously.
[00:28:13] Raj: Any guidance on scheduling when multiple models are served? We run summarization and a smaller reranker.
[00:28:18] Priya: Prefer model-specific queues, let the scheduler treat them separately. Rerankers (small models) can be placed on CPU or small GPUs to avoid interfering with the big-gen models. Also create prioritization rules so critical user-facing routes get preference.
[00:28:30] [00:34:55] Unidentified Participant: Quick question — is there an automated tuner?
[00:35:00] Priya: We have an Optimize feature that suggests initial knobs based on traces and gives expected delta columns. It is prescriptive, but for on‑prem you often need iterative manual runs because network/topology differs.
[00:35:09] Evan: We'll run the Optimize suggestion as a baseline and then do 1–2 manual passes with you.
[00:35:15] Tom: What logs should we attach when we run the stress test?
[00:35:18] Priya: Scheduler logs, per-batch composition, kv hit/miss logs, GPU utilization and per-device memory, and OS-level network tail latencies. Also the token distribution CSV Sara mentioned.
[00:35:28] Sara: We'll produce those.
[00:35:35] [00:41:02] Priya: Final notes on graceful degradation: set model-fallback chains and serve a compressed/quantized model for low-priority workloads when capacity is constrained. Also configure a slow-path queue for very long contexts and stream partial results to UX so it doesn't look like a stall.
[00:41:16] Raj: For the slow-path can you recommend a user-visible UX pattern?
[00:41:20] Priya: Show a partial transcript with a progress indicator and sticky session ID so later chunks append. That reduces user frustration.
[00:41:30] Evan: We'll attach a UX pattern doc.
[00:41:34] [00:48:55] Closing / recap:
- Redwood to send knob playbook + sample helm values + pre-warm script + quantization note (Evan/Priya)
- Customer to run warm-cache 1-hour stress test and upload logs (Sara/Tom)
